questions.question: What are the most useful string operations in Ruby?
questions.title: String Operations in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Ruby strings have rich methods. Inspection: s.length, s.empty?, s.include?('sub'). Transformation: s.upcase, s.downcase, s.capitalize, s.swapcase, s.reverse, s.strip (trim whitespace), s.chomp (remove trailing newline). Split/join: s.split(',') -> array; s.split(/\s+/) on whitespace; arr.join('-') -> string. Replace: s.gsub('a', 'b') (all), s.sub (first), s.gsub(/\d/) { |d| d.to_i*2 }. Access: s[0], s[-1], s[0..2] (slice), s.start_with?('a'), s.end_with?('.rb'). Convert: s.to_i, s.to_f, s.to_sym, 42.to_s. Many return new strings (upcase); bang versions mutate in place (upcase!). Strings are mutable by default (frozen_string_literal: true makes them immutable). Use + or << to concatenate, * to repeat ('ab' * 3 == 'ababab').

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know upcase/downcase/strip/reverse, split/join, gsub, and the bang-version distinction.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting gsub returns a new string (use gsub! to mutate), or chomp vs strip (chomp removes only trailing newline).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: String ops: length/empty?/include?; upcase/downcase/strip/reverse; split/join; gsub/sub; s[0..2]; to_i/to_s. Bang versions mutate.

inspect/transform/split/join/gsub; bang versions mutate. ab*3=ababab.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[string] --> I[length/empty?/include?]
  S --> T[upcase/strip/reverse]
  S --> Sp[split / join]
  S --> G[gsub: replace]
  T --> B[! versions mutate]
```

sections.title: String operations
sections.content:
```ruby
s = '  Hello, World  '

# Inspection
s.length            # 15
s.empty?            # false
s.include?('World') # true

# Transformation (return NEW string)
s.strip             # 'Hello, World'   (trim whitespace)
s.upcase            # '  HELLO, WORLD  '
s.downcase          # '  hello, world  '
s.reverse           # '  dlroW ,olleH  '
s.chomp             # remove trailing NEWLINE only

# Bang versions MUTATE in place:
s2 = 'hi'; s2.upcase!; s2  # 'HI'

# Split / Join
'a,b,c'.split(',')         # ['a','b','c']
'one two three'.split(/\s+/)  # ['one','two','three']
['a','b'].join('-')        # 'a-b'

# Replace
'hello'.gsub('l', 'L')      # 'heLLo' (all)
'hello'.sub('l', 'L')       # 'heLlo' (first only)
'a1b2'.gsub(/\d/) { |d| d.to_i * 2 }  # 'a2b4'

# Access / slice
s = 'hello'
s[0]              # 'h'
s[-1]             # 'o' (negative from end)
s[0..2]           # 'hel' (slice, inclusive)
s.start_with?('he')  # true
s.end_with?('lo')    # true

# Convert
'42'.to_i         # 42
'3.14'.to_f       # 3.14
'x'.to_sym        # :x
42.to_s           # '42'

# Concatenate / repeat
'ab' + 'cd'       # 'abcd'
'ab' << 'cd'      # 'abcd' (<< mutates)
'ab' * 3          # 'ababab'
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting gsub returns a new string (use gsub! to mutate).
chomp vs strip: chomp removes only a trailing newline; strip removes all whitespace.
Forgetting negative indices (s[-1] is the last char).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Inspection: length, empty?, include?; transformation: upcase/downcase/strip/reverse/chomp.
Replace: sub (first), gsub (all); gsub can take a regex and a block.
Bang versions (upcase!, gsub!) mutate in place; + / << concatenate; * repeats.
